title: 1 Samuel 7:1–4
context: The men of Kiriath Jearim come and take the LORD’s ark into Abinadab’s house on the hill, and they consecrate Eleazar his son to keep it. From the day the ark stayed there, the time was long—for it was twenty years—and all the house of Israel lamented after the LORD. Samuel then speaks to all the house of Israel: if they are returning to the LORD with all their heart, they must put away the foreign gods and the Ashtaroth from among them, direct their hearts to the LORD, and serve him only, and he will deliver them out of the hand of the Philistines. The children of Israel remove the Baals and the Ashtaroth and serve the LORD only. Both traditions read the unit as the turn from housing the ark to a public, wholehearted return. The twenty years names a long stay; it is often read as the span that leads to this lament and this repentance, not necessarily as a complete chronology down to the ark’s later removal, and that question need not be settled here. Repentance and the promise of the LORD’s deliverance are shared ground: the idols must go, the heart must be directed to the LORD, and he is the one who will save.

verses.text: The men of Kiriath Jearim came and took the LORD’s ark, and brought it into Abinadab’s house on the hill, and consecrated Eleazar his son to keep the LORD’s ark.
verses.arminianNotes:
The men of Kiriath Jearim came and took the LORD’s ark, and brought it into Abinadab’s house on the hill, and consecrated Eleazar his son to keep the LORD’s ark. The request of 6:21 is answered by a household set apart to watch over it.

Arminian readers hear a real receiving and a real consecration. Eleazar is set apart to keep the ark; the hill and the house are as the WEB names them. The ark is not left without a keeper.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise take the bringing up to Abinadab’s house and the consecration of Eleazar as the narrator’s account of a guarded rest for the ark. It remains the LORD’s ark, now kept in an Israelite house on the hill.

Both traditions read the verse as the ark’s new lodging, shared ground, without a contrast over Abinadab’s later story. The text here simply names the house and the son.

verses.text: From the day that the ark stayed in Kiriath Jearim, the time was long—for it was twenty years; and all the house of Israel lamented after the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes:
From the day that the ark stayed in Kiriath Jearim, “the time was long—for it was twenty years;” and all the house of Israel “lamented after the LORD.” A long stay and a national lament prepare Samuel’s call.

Arminian readers hear a real waiting and a real grief directed toward the LORD. Twenty years is a long time; the lament is the soil in which the returning of the next verses can take place. The figure is the span the narrator names for this period of staying and lamenting, not a full timetable of every later movement of the ark.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress the same long time and the same lament after the LORD. The ark is present in Kiriath Jearim, and still the house of Israel must be called to return; presence of the ark has not by itself produced exclusive service.

Both traditions take the twenty years and the lament as the hinge into Samuel’s word, shared ground, without forcing a single solution to later chronological questions.

verses.text: Samuel spoke to all the house of Israel, saying, “If you are returning to the LORD with all your heart, then put away the foreign gods and the Ashtaroth from among you, and direct your hearts to the LORD, and serve him only; and he will deliver you out of the hand of the Philistines.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Samuel spoke to all the house of Israel, saying, “If you are returning to the LORD with all your heart, then put away the foreign gods and the Ashtaroth from among you, and direct your hearts to the LORD, and serve him only; and he will deliver you out of the hand of the Philistines.”

Arminian readers hear a genuine call with a genuine promise. If they return with all the heart, put the gods away, direct their hearts, and serve him only, he will deliver them. The condition is not theater; they must actually do this, and the deliverance is the LORD’s.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress the same exclusive service and the same promise of deliverance. Samuel’s “If” is the way a whole people is summoned to put away the Baals and to serve the LORD only; the rescue from the Philistines will be God’s doing, not the fruit of a half turn.

Both traditions take repentance and the LORD’s help as shared ground here. There is no deliverance promised while the foreign gods remain, and no contrast need be forced over the word “If”.

verses.text: Then the children of Israel removed the Baals and the Ashtaroth, and served the LORD only.
verses.arminianNotes:
Then the children of Israel removed the Baals and the Ashtaroth, “and served the LORD only.” They do what Samuel required: the gods are put away, and the service is exclusive.

Arminian readers hear a real obedience. The return is visible in the removal of the Baals and the Ashtaroth and in serving the LORD only; this is the repentance the next assembly at Mizpah will deepen, not a mere slogan.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise take the verse as the people’s actual response to Samuel’s word. The Baals and the Ashtaroth are removed, and the LORD alone is served, the condition on which deliverance was promised.

Both traditions read the verse as shared ground of concrete repentance. The idols are not renamed or kept in reserve; they are put away, and the LORD is served only.
